title: NDPS special courts - how trial timelines actually work
p1: A case under the NDPS Act can feel like it moves at a completely different speed. But do special courts really mean instant trials? The answer surprises many people.
p2: A common belief is that because NDPS cases go before special courts, the trial must finish quickly. In reality, special courts are created to handle these cases efficiently, but they still follow legal steps like evidence recording, witness examination, cross-examination, and arguments. A delay does not automatically mean the court is ignoring the case.
p3: The timeline depends on many moving parts: the number of witnesses, availability of records, forensic reports, custody issues, and whether either side seeks adjournments. One thing many people don't know: even a special court cannot skip mandatory procedures just to complete a trial faster. The goal is a fair trial, not merely a fast one. A practical takeaway is that every NDPS case timeline is shaped by its facts, not just by the name of the court handling it.
conclusion: Do you think special courts should have fixed deadlines for NDPS trials, or would that risk affecting a fair hearing?
